tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Mia avoids talking on the phone while she cycles through traffic.
The twins enjoy to bake cinnamon rolls on rainy Sundays.
After the match, the coach decided postponing the next training session.
Noah refused to share his notes before the chemistry quiz.
Lara promised delivering the costumes for the school play by Thursday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid takes a gerund, so "avoids talking" is the natural pattern.

Tip: Memorise avoid + -ing; an infinitive after avoid is almost always wrong.

FALSE — Enjoy needs a gerund, not an infinitive: "enjoy baking," not "enjoy to bake."

Tip: Like, love, and enjoy prefer -ing when the object is an activity.

FALSE — Decide takes a to-infinitive: "decided to postpone," not a gerund.

Tip: Decide / refuse / promise / plan / hope / expect pattern with to + base verb.

TRUE — Refuse correctly takes a to-infinitive: "refuse to share."

Tip: If the meaning is "will not do X," expect refuse + to-infinitive.

FALSE — Promise takes a to-infinitive: "promised to deliver," not a gerund.

Tip: Promise patterns like decide and refuse — to + verb, not -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: This set drills the core split: avoid and enjoy need -ing, while decide, refuse, and promise need to + verb. Check each verb's fixed pattern before you judge the sentence.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The hiking club is considering organising a dawn walk next month.
Sofia enjoys reading graphic novels on the train.
The family decided to camp beside the lake this weekend.
The barista refused accepting tips during the charity day.
Jamal promised to text when his flight landed.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Consider takes a gerund: "considering organising" is correct.

Tip: Consider / avoid / enjoy / finish / suggest all take -ing when followed by a verb.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund is the standard pattern: "enjoy reading."

Tip: If enjoy is followed by an activity, use -ing, not to.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to camp."

Tip: Decision verbs (decide, agree, refuse, promise) lean toward to + base verb.

FALSE — Refuse needs a to-infinitive: "refused to accept," not a gerund.

Tip: Swap -ing for to + verb after refuse and the sentence usually repairs itself.

TRUE — Promise correctly takes a to-infinitive: "promised to text."

Tip: Promise + to-infinitive expresses a future commitment.
tasks.solution_overview: Four verbs here follow their textbook patterns correctly; only refuse is broken. Treat refuse like decide and promise — always to + verb.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The librarian avoided to mention the overdue fines in front of the class.
Trainee chefs enjoy to practise knife skills on quiet mornings.
Management is considering to outsource the school canteen.
The band decided expanding their tour into two neighbouring towns.
The driver refused to open the boot without seeing ID.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Avoid needs -ing: "avoided mentioning," not "avoided to mention."

Tip: Avoid + gerund is fixed; do not borrow the to-infinitive from decide/promise.

FALSE — Enjoy takes a gerund: "enjoy practising."

Tip: Enjoy / avoid / consider share the -ing pattern.

FALSE — Consider takes -ing: "considering outsourcing."

Tip: If you can swap in "the idea of …ing," you want a gerund after consider.

FALSE — Decide needs to + verb: "decided to expand."

Tip: Decide never takes a bare gerund as its complement.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive is correct: "refused to open."

Tip: Refusal language almost always pairs with to + base verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Four classic wrong-pattern lines and one clean refuse + to. Flip every avoid/enjoy/consider error to -ing and every decide error to to + verb.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We stopped to buy ice cream when we reached the pier.
Please stop to chew gum during the recital.
On the motorway they stopped talking and listened to the news.
She stopped to smoking after her doctor warned her.
He stopped typing when the fire alarm sounded.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive means pause in order to do something else: they interrupted the journey to buy ice cream.

Tip: Stop to = interrupt activity A so you can do activity B.

FALSE — Here you want quit the habit: "stop chewing," not "stop to chew."

Tip: Stop -ing = quit / no longer do that activity.

TRUE — Stop + gerund means they quit talking.

Tip: If the meaning is "no longer do X," use stop + -ing.

FALSE — Habit quitting needs the gerund: "stopped smoking," not "stopped to smoking."

Tip: Never mix to and -ing after stop in the same slot.

TRUE — Stop + gerund correctly means he quit typing when the alarm rang.

Tip: Sudden interruption of the same action → stop + -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: Stop changes meaning with form: stop to = pause in order to; stop -ing = quit the activity. Ask which sense the sentence needs before you mark it.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Athletes often avoid eating heavy meals right before a race.
My grandparents enjoy gardening in the late afternoon.
Have you considered joining the community choir?
Elena decided studying abroad for one semester.
The museum promised to reopen the sculpture wing in May.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoid eating."

Tip: Health and habit advice often uses avoid + -ing.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund names a liked activity: "enjoy gardening."

Tip: Enjoy almost never takes to + verb in standard English.

TRUE — Consider + gerund is correct: "considered joining."

Tip: Consider = think about doing → -ing.

FALSE — Decide needs to + verb: "decided to study."

Tip: Decide / choose / refuse / promise → to-infinitive.

TRUE — Promise + to-infinitive is correct: "promised to reopen."

Tip: Commitments after promise use to + base verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Clean models for avoid, enjoy, consider, and promise sit beside one decide error. Keep the -ing trio separate from the to-infinitive trio.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Tourists should avoid to swim near the rocks after dark.
Kids usually enjoy building sandcastles at low tide.
We are considering to rent bikes for the coastal path.
The jury refused to discuss the case outside the room.
Dad promised calling us as soon as the ferry docked.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Avoid takes -ing: "avoid swimming."

Tip: Warnings with avoid always want the gerund.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund is correct: "enjoy building."

Tip: Enjoy + activity = -ing every time.

FALSE — Consider takes -ing: "considering renting."

Tip: Consider to + verb is a frequent exam trap — reject it.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive is correct: "refused to discuss."

Tip: Refuse patterns with decide and promise.

FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promised to call."

Tip: Promise + -ing is not standard for future commitments.
tasks.solution_overview: Two clean lines (enjoy, refuse) and three pattern flips. Watch especially avoid/consider + to and promise + -ing.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Runners stopped to stretch at the water station.
Please stop shouting; the neighbours can hear you.
We stopped for buying tickets at the kiosk.
She stopped to check the map because the path forked.
He stopped to listen music and missed the announcement.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop to stretch = pause the run in order to stretch.

Tip: Purpose after an interruption → stop + to-infinitive.

TRUE — Stop shouting = quit the noisy behaviour.

Tip: Quit an ongoing action → stop + -ing.

FALSE — After stop, use to + verb for purpose, not for + -ing: "stopped to buy tickets."

Tip: For + -ing after stop is not the purpose pattern you want here.

TRUE — Stop to check = interrupt travel in order to check the map.

Tip: Reason/purpose after pause → to-infinitive.

FALSE — Listen needs to: "stopped listening to music" (quit) or "stopped to listen to music" (pause in order to). As written, both form and preposition fail.

Tip: After stop, choose to or -ing by meaning — and keep listen to intact.
tasks.solution_overview: Deepen the stop contrast and catch side traps like for + -ing and missing to after listen. Meaning still decides between to and -ing.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I avoid checking social media before breakfast.
They enjoy to watch documentaries about deep-sea life.
Have you considered changing your route to avoid the roadworks?
The committee decided to cancel the outdoor picnic.
She refused helping with the dishes until her homework was done.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoid checking."

Tip: Avoid + -ing for habits you try not to do.

FALSE — Enjoy needs -ing: "enjoy watching."

Tip: Enjoy to + verb is almost never right.

TRUE — Consider + gerund is correct: "considered changing."

Tip: Consider = weigh an option → -ing.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to cancel."

Tip: Decisions about future actions take to + verb.

FALSE — Refuse needs to + verb: "refused to help."

Tip: Refuse + -ing is a classic false friend with avoid/enjoy.
tasks.solution_overview: Mix of clean avoid/consider/decide lines and two flips (enjoy to, refuse -ing). Group the verbs by pattern before scoring.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: After years of late nights, he finally stopped drinking energy drinks.
We stopped to ask a local which tram went to the museum.
They stopped to arguing when the teacher walked in.
She never enjoys waiting in long airport queues.
The cast promised rehearsing every evening until opening night.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + gerund = quit the habit of drinking energy drinks.

Tip: Habit change → stop + -ing.

TRUE — Stop to ask = pause the journey in order to ask.

Tip: Purpose after a pause → stop + to.

FALSE — Quit arguing needs the gerund alone: "stopped arguing," not "stopped to arguing."

Tip: Do not glue to onto a gerund after stop.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund is correct (here negated): "enjoys waiting."

Tip: Negation does not change the enjoy + -ing pattern.

FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promised to rehearse."

Tip: Promise + -ing fails the commitment pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Stop meaning splits again, plus a hybrid "to arguing" error and a promise trap. Keep purpose (to) versus cessation (-ing) sharply separate.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Passengers should avoid blocking the aisle with large suitcases.
Would you consider to volunteer at the food bank this winter?
The captain decided to turn back because of the fog.
My brother refuses admitting he lost the house keys.
Aunt Priya enjoys knitting scarves for the whole family.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoid blocking."

Tip: Public notices often use avoid + -ing.

FALSE — Consider takes -ing: "consider volunteering."

Tip: Consider to is a frequent trap — rewrite with -ing.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to turn."

Tip: Sudden decisions still take to + verb.

FALSE — Refuse needs to + verb: "refuses to admit."

Tip: Refuse + -ing mimics avoid wrongly — flip it.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund is correct: "enjoys knitting."

Tip: Hobby verbs after enjoy always take -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: Three solid models and two crossed patterns (consider to, refuse -ing). Sort each verb into the -ing list or the to list before you answer.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We decided not to climb the ridge after the weather warning.
She avoids not to sit near the speakers at concerts.
They refused not to apologise, even though everyone expected it.
He promised not to spoil the ending of the film.
I enjoy not waking up to an alarm on Sundays.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Decide + not + to-infinitive is the correct negation: "decided not to climb."

Tip: Negate the infinitive with not before to, not with a gerund.

FALSE — Avoid already means "not do"; use "avoids sitting," not "avoids not to sit."

Tip: Avoid + -ing; do not stack an extra not + to.

FALSE — The intended sense is almost always "refused to apologise" (would not apologise). "Refused not to apologise" is a double negative mess.

Tip: Refuse + to + verb; put not only when you truly mean "refuse to not do X."

TRUE — Promise + not + to-infinitive is correct: "promised not to spoil."

Tip: Negation sits before to in the infinitive pattern.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund works with negation inside the activity: "enjoy not waking."

Tip: Enjoy still wants -ing even when the activity is a negative state.
tasks.solution_overview: Negation tests the same fixed patterns: not to after decide/promise, plain -ing after avoid/enjoy, and careful handling of refuse.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Midway through the hike we stopped drinking from the stream and switched to bottled water.
Midway through the hike we stopped to drink from our bottles.
The guide stopped us from approaching the cliff edge.
Please stop to interrupting the speaker with side comments.
They stopped singing as soon as the conductor raised her hand.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + gerund = quit the activity of drinking from the stream.

Tip: Same action ends → stop + -ing.

TRUE — Stop to drink = pause walking in order to drink.

Tip: Purpose of the pause → stop + to.

TRUE — Stop someone from + -ing is a related but valid pattern: prevent them from doing X.

Tip: Stop + object + from + -ing = prevent.

FALSE — Quit interrupting needs "stop interrupting," not "stop to interrupting."

Tip: Never attach to directly to an -ing form after stop.

TRUE — Stop + gerund = they quit singing on cue.

Tip: Instant cessation of the same action → -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: Pair stop to / stop -ing with the prevent pattern stop someone from -ing, and reject the hybrid "to interrupting."

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having considered moving house, they decided to stay another year.
She enjoys to be the first to arrive at rehearsals.
We avoided discussing politics at the family dinner.
He refused being photographed without his consent.
The mayor promised to fund the new skate park next spring.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Consider + gerund and decide + to-infinitive both follow their fixed patterns in one sentence.

Tip: Different verbs in the same sentence can still keep their own complements.

FALSE — Enjoy needs -ing: "enjoys being."

Tip: Enjoy + being / doing, never enjoy to be in this sense.

TRUE — Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoided discussing."

Tip: Sensitive topics often pair with avoid + -ing.

FALSE — Refuse needs to + verb: "refused to be photographed."

Tip: Passive infinitives still follow refuse + to.

TRUE — Promise + to-infinitive is correct: "promised to fund."

Tip: Public commitments use promise + to.
tasks.solution_overview: Stacked verbs, a passive after refuse, and an enjoy trap. Track each verb's complement independently.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I never stop to wonder how the magician hid the coin.
I never stop wondering how the magician hid the coin.
Doctors advised him to stop to smoke immediately.
They decided against postponing the wedding.
She is considering whether to accept the internship offer.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The intended idiom is continuous curiosity: "never stop wondering" (gerund), not pause-in-order-to wonder.

Tip: Never stop + -ing = keep doing something all the time.

TRUE — Never stop + gerund correctly means the wondering continues.

Tip: Idiomatic "can't/never stop -ing" always wants the gerund.

FALSE — Quit smoking needs "stop smoking"; "stop to smoke" would mean pause something else in order to smoke.

Tip: Medical advice to quit → stop + -ing.

TRUE — Decide against + gerund is a valid related pattern: "decided against postponing."

Tip: Decide to + verb OR decide against + -ing.

TRUE — Consider whether + to-infinitive is grammatical when whether introduces the option.

Tip: Bare consider + verb → -ing; consider whether → to is fine.
tasks.solution_overview: Idioms and near-neighbours: never stop -ing, stop smoking vs stop to smoke, decide against -ing, and consider whether to.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Rather than argue, they decided to sleep on the problem.
She avoids to be seen wearing the same outfit twice.
We enjoy being invited to their rooftop barbecues.
He refused to let the puppy sleep on the sofa.
The club promised arranging free coaching for beginners.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to sleep."

Tip: Rather than does not change decide's to-pattern.

FALSE — Avoid needs -ing: "avoids being seen."

Tip: Passive gerunds still follow avoid + -ing.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund (passive) is correct: "enjoy being invited."

Tip: Enjoy + being + past participle is a common natural pattern.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive is correct: "refused to let."

Tip: Refuse to let / refuse to allow keep the to.

FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promised to arrange."

Tip: Promise + -ing is still wrong even with a kind offer.
tasks.solution_overview: Passive gerunds after avoid/enjoy and a promise error. Form (active/passive) does not rewrite the verb's complement rule.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: What made them stop to check the tyre pressure was a strange vibration.
What made them stop checking their phones was the no-device rule.
Investors are considering selling a small stake in the start-up.
She decided that postponing the trip would be wiser.
He enjoys when friends drop by without calling first.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop to check = pause driving in order to check the tyres.

Tip: Cleft "what made them…" still keeps stop's meaning split.

TRUE — Stop checking = quit the phone-checking habit.

Tip: Same cleft frame, opposite stop pattern — meaning decides.

TRUE — Consider + gerund is correct (one rare finance-tinged line): "considering selling."

Tip: Even in money contexts, consider still wants -ing.

TRUE — Decide that + clause is grammatical; the gerund postponing is the subject of the that-clause, not decide's complement.

Tip: Decide to + verb OR decide that + clause — both work.

TRUE — Enjoy can take a when-clause as its object; no verb-complement conflict arises.

Tip: Enjoy + noun/gerund/clause — but not enjoy to + verb.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are sound once you separate stop's two meanings and allow decide that / enjoy when as alternative structures.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Far from avoiding to answer, she volunteered the awkward detail first.
They kept promising finishing the mural before the festival.
Only after refusing to compromise did the two sides walk out.
Having enjoyed to sail as children, they booked a dinghy again.
Stop to pretend you did not hear the question.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Avoid still needs -ing: "avoiding answering."

Tip: Far from + -ing does not license avoid + to.

FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promising to finish."

Tip: Keep / start do not change promise's to-pattern.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive is correct inside the inversion: "refusing to compromise."

Tip: Inversion and emphasis leave the refuse + to pattern intact.

FALSE — Enjoy needs -ing: "enjoyed sailing."

Tip: Perfect participle having enjoyed still takes -ing.

FALSE — Quit pretending needs "stop pretending," not "stop to pretend" (which would mean pause in order to pretend).

Tip: Commands to quit an act → stop + -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: Hard wrappers (far from, keep -ing, inversion, having -ed) still cannot rewrite avoid/enjoy/promise/stop. Only refuse to survives cleanly.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She stopped to mean that she was leaving; she simply paused for breath.
If you stop meaning what you say, people stop trusting you.
We are still considering how to phrase the apology.
He decided on renting the attic flat above the bakery.
They refused their friends' offer of driving them home.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Nonsense meaning: stop to mean is not English for "intend." Use "She did not mean…" or similar.

Tip: Stop to only works when the infinitive is a real purpose action.

TRUE — Stop + gerund twice: quit meaning X / quit trusting Y.

Tip: Parallel stop + -ing structures keep the "cease" sense.

TRUE — Consider + how + to-infinitive is fine when how introduces the method.

Tip: Consider + -ing OR consider + wh-word + to.

TRUE — Decide on + gerund/noun is a valid alternative to decide to + verb.

Tip: Decide to go OR decide on going — both grammatical.

TRUE — Refuse can take a noun object ("refused their friends' offer"); the of + -ing belongs to offer, not to refuse.

Tip: Refuse + noun and refuse + to + verb are both correct.
tasks.solution_overview: Edge grammar: impossible stop to mean, parallel stop -ing, consider how to, decide on -ing, and refuse + noun. Look past the first verb when the complement sits elsewhere.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not wishing to appear rude, she avoided interrupting the poet mid-line.
Not wishing to appear rude, she avoided to interrupt the poet mid-line.
They promised that they would water the plants while we were away.
He enjoys that his sister always remembers his birthday.
We stopped short of promising to host the entire reunion.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoided interrupting."

Tip: Fronted participle clauses do not change avoid's -ing rule.

FALSE — Same sentence with the wrong complement: avoid needs -ing, not to.

Tip: Compare the pair; only the gerund version works.

TRUE — Promise that + clause is a valid alternative to promise to + verb.

Tip: Promise to water OR promise that we will water.

TRUE — Enjoy that + clause is acceptable; the that-clause is the object.

Tip: Enjoy + -ing for activities; enjoy that for facts/situations.

TRUE — Stop short of + -ing is an idiom meaning "almost but not quite"; promising keeps its own to.

Tip: Idioms can nest: stop short of + gerund, and inside it promise + to.
tasks.solution_overview: Minimal pairs, that-clause alternatives, and the idiom stop short of -ing. Confirm which structure is actually complementing which verb.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Had they considered postponing, they might have decided to wait for clearer skies.
She cannot help enjoying to win, even in friendly matches.
Whatever they refuse to discuss in public, they still avoid lying to each other.
To stop to worry is not the same as to stop worrying.
Only those who promise delivering results on time keep their places on the team.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Consider + gerund and decide + to-infinitive both correct inside a conditional.

Tip: Complex syntax still respects each verb's fixed complement.

FALSE — Enjoy needs -ing: "enjoying winning" (and cannot help + -ing is itself a gerund pattern).

Tip: Nested -ing does not license enjoy to.

TRUE — Refuse + to and avoid + -ing both correct in parallel clauses.

Tip: Different verbs, different complements — both can be right at once.

TRUE — The contrast is precisely the teaching point: stop to worry ≠ stop worrying.

Tip: Infinitive subjects can showcase the stop meaning split cleanly.

FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promise to deliver."

Tip: Relative clauses do not unlock promise + -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: Final stress test: stacked patterns, cannot help + enjoy, parallel refuse/avoid, the stop meaning contrast as subject, and a last promise trap.
